title: 8 Ways To Fuel Your Students’ Intrinsic Motivation
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that most students are praised too often and too extravagantly, which paradoxically erodes work ethic by lowering the bar for what counts as praiseworthy. He offers eight guidelines for praise that genuinely fuels intrinsic motivation: making it deserved, subtle, private, silent, written, belated, based on unrealized potential, and occasionally joyous when warranted. Throughout, he emphasizes that praise only holds meaning when earned through real effort, and that subtle, low-key acknowledgment — a note, a nod, a quiet word — often carries more motivational power than public celebration. He closes by cautioning that praise should never be withheld from true accomplishment, only reserved for it.
points: Over-praising students for ordinary, unearned achievements is argued to erode work ethic rather than build motivation.
Praise should be deserved, tied to real achievement defined individually for each student, to hold any lasting meaning.
Subtle and private forms of praise — eye contact, a nod, a handwritten note — are described as more motivationally powerful than public celebration.
Belated praise, delivered unexpectedly after the fact, can be especially impactful because it feels unprompted and genuine.
Praise based on untapped potential, delivered honestly and directly, is offered as a way to push capable students toward higher performance.
quotes: For every time you praise students for something that didn’t involve hard work or a certain mental toughness to accomplish, a sliver of their dignity is taken from them.

When a teacher refrains from giving praise for doing what is expected, however, and instead keeps her eyes pealed for true accomplishment, she adds a jolt of fuel to her students’ intrinsic motivation.

Small, subtle gestures of praise are among the most effective. Mere eye contact from across the room, carefully timed, one-word recognition, a single nod of the head—they can send a student’s internal motivation into hyper drive.
A stationery note, written in your careful hand, folded over and stuck to the inside of a student’s desk is perhaps the most effective form of praise you could ever use.

If you witness them stepping beyond what are common expectations and into the realm of true accomplishment, don’t let them hang there on the vine unnoticed, where the fruit of excellence withers and dies.
